newsitem.title: USA: CD-ROMs Offer Better Betting and 'Batman'.
newsitem.headline: CD-ROMs Offer Better Betting and 'Batman'.

text.p: During a trip to Las Vegas for the Consumer Electronics Show, I shared a courtesy limousine ride with a gentleman who explained how easy it was to win at the casinos. You simply cash out while you're ahead, he said, and you can regularly make money.
I didn't have the heart to ask him why, if it's so easy, he was driving the limo.
If you are one of those people who steadfastly believes you can beat the odds, or you want to get a sense of what it takes to win (or lose) money at a casino, two recently released CD-ROMs may help.

"Avery Cardoza's Casino" (Cardoza Entertainment, Windows, $50) is designed to teach players winning strategies (or at least, how to lose less rapidly). At any point, while you're playing blackjack, craps, slots, keno, roulette or video poker, you click on the "expert" button to get instant advice about how to make the best play in that situation.
It gives novices a quick appreciation of where the good and bad bets are.

For example, I tried a video poker machine where deuces were wild. When I was dealt a hand whose best cards were a deuce and an ace, my initial inclination was to keep both of those cards and draw three new ones. But in that particular brand of video poker, it's wisest to keep only the deuce in hopes that you'll get another deuce, producing an automatic three-of-a-kind, the minimum combination for a payout. "Cardoza's Casino" shows how the strategy should vary depending on the rules of each machine.
The instruction booklet teaches some card counting skills, but it doesn't let you practice in a true-to-life way because you're the only one at the blackjack table.

A few things bothered me about "Cardoza's Casino." Cardoza's strategy guide for the CD-ROM often seems to be designed to entice hopeful players to send away for other gambling products that are supposed to increase their odds even more. (His 30-page catalogue of gambling books, strategies, software and accessories is included).

After he teaches you about card counting, for example, he reveals he has a strategy that works without counting cards and gives players an edge of about one-half percent to 1 percent. Price: $55 (with coupon).

The real question is whether these strategies really help you beat the odds. I wasn't encouraged when I found that the strategy guide included with the game advertises a $150 software package that claims to be able to help you win the lottery, a claim that most statisticians would strongly question.
It makes you wonder if one of the goals of this CD-ROM is to insure that America never has a shortage of skilled limousine drivers.
"Golden Nugget" (Virgin Interactive, Windows95, $40) lets you play all the games in "Cardoza's Casino," plus a few more, including Pai Gow Poker, 5 Card Texas Hold 'Em and 7 Card Stud.

It also has the look and sound of a real Las Vegas casino, a sense of realism that is shattered when you look around and realise that the sounds of a crowded casino are coming from a room that is completely empty.
This game takes your money without the benefit of expert help.

Although a lot less time is required to load the game (the Cardoza product can be pretty slow), "Golden Nugget"'s blackjack hands are dealt much more slowly than those in "Cardoza's Casino," in part because you're sharing the table with three other people.

Like "Cardoza's Casino," "Golden Nugget" lets you play casino games without having to risk losing real money. Unlike "Cardoza's," "Golden Nugget" doesn't hold out any questionable promises that you can be a winner in a real casino.
It also has a campy role-playing game involving a mysterious message encrypted in Piglatin and a missing "chaos computer chip" capable of predicting seemingly-random events using the chaos theory.
The game features Adam West of the old "Batman" television series, whose performance makes you suspect that millionaire Bruce Wayne has changed his name and moved to Las Vegas.

"Crime never folds a hand when justice is holding a pair of deuces," he tells you at one point. And when he suddenly gets a flash of inspiration that will send him to his crime laboratory, West announces, "Quick! To the elevators!" with precisely the same tone he once used to proclaim, "Quick! To the Batcave!"
The only thing that's missing is Robin. I'm told he now drives a limo.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
